text: FELLOWSHIP OF THE HEART Going Out series Going Out The body sent — witness as the missional outworking of formation FORMATION COMPANION HANDBOOK Pilot edition — Covenant Christian Academy of Warrenton Based on the Intentional Journey of the Heart (IJH), Volumes 1–6 John G. Tittle • Curriculum draft v1, June 2026 A Letter to the Companion Welcome to the third movement. This handbook is for the team carrying the Going Out series at Covenant Christian Academy of Warrenton. Most of you have walked Getting Started and Going Deeper with these families. Some of you are coming in fresh because the work has grown and we need depth on the team — Companions whose own walk and pastoral capacity match the demands of Going Out, regardless of chronological age. The handbook uses the role names Lead Companion, Cohort Companion, Co Companion, and pastoral support throughout, drawing on Vol 5's formation companion architecture rather than congregational elder language. The handbook is written for both of you. Going Out is not curriculum. It is the missional outworking of what the Spirit has already been forming across two prior series. Getting Started introduced the vocabulary and the four Connects. Going Deeper did the diagnostic and therapeutic work of Vol 2 — soils, knots, lies, confession, hearing, gifts, shadow, calling. Going Out engages what all of that was for : a body sent into the world to bear witness. The same Spirit who formed the cohort inwardly now sends it outward. Three things you should know before you read further. First: Going Out is about being sent into your actual life — your household, your work, your third places, and wherever else the Spirit has prepared good works for you to walk in. It is not, primarily, about starting something new. Most of this cohort will be sent more deeply into the rooms they already occupy. The witness is ordinary before it is ever extraordinary, and the ordinary is the point. Second: not every calling looks the same, and the series is built to honor that honestly. When the cohort discerns together at Week 8 where each member is being sent, the honest landings are several — a deepening in the household, a vocational long obedience, a sustained third place arc, a one to one accompaniment, a contemplative and largely hidden shape, and yes, sometimes a calling to gather a new formation group. These are not a hierarchy. The body that hears "stay and go deeper where you are" has heard just as truly as the body that hears "go and gather." The team's discipline is to hold all of these as equally real. Third: the specific calling to start a new formation group has its own follow on. Going Out discerns and confirms that calling where it is present; it does not, by itself, equip it. The equipping — the spiritual authority architecture, the leadership taxonomy, the first session work — lives in the companion handbook Inviting Others , which runs after Going Out for those whose Week 8 discernment surfaced the group starting direction. Keep the two distinct in your own mind and in the cohort's: Going Out is the volume every graduate walks; Inviting Others is the follow on a few are called into. Walk gently. The people in this room have given you two series of honest formation work. Going Out asks them to carry that work out the door into the rooms where they are most known and least able to perform — and that is harder, not easier, than the interior work was. Honor what they have given you by sending them honestly into what is actually theirs. The work itself is the Spirit's; we are the room He is using to confirm and send what He has already begun. — John A note on the three Level taxonomies in the IJH corpus. Three different five level frameworks operate in the FotH curriculum, and they share the surface vocabulary "Level 1 … Level 5." On first reading they can be confusing. Each is theologically distinct and addresses a different unit of formation. Affective Taxonomy (educational psychology; Vol 2 Exp 7)

title: Going Out
text: Going Out Twelve Tuesdays. The body sent — witness as the missional outworking of formation, in the household, the workplace, the third place, and beyond. The third of the three Fellowship of the Heart series. Twelve ninety minute sessions for the cohort that has walked Getting Started and Going Deeper and is now being prepared, individually and as a body, for what comes next. Going Out is not curriculum . It is the missional outworking of what the Spirit has already formed across two prior series — the body sent into ordinary witness in the rooms it already occupies, discerning together, at Week 8, where each member is being sent. These files are the Companion Lesson Plans — what the Lead Companion and Co Companion team hold during the session. The twelve weeks Title Focus 1 Welcome Back — Returning to the Sent Body Re open the cohort; name the interlude; orient outward 2 The Body Sent What it means to be a sent body, not a sequestered one 3 Where Sent The four contexts: household, vocational, third place, beyond 4 Daily Tells The weekly practice of telling outside the cohort 5 Household Sent into the household 6 Vocational Sent into the vocational context 7 Third Place Sent into the third place 8 Discernment The cohort discerns together where each member is sent 9 The Body Sent Beyond The cohort beyond its own life 10 What Going Out Produced What was formed; what is being sent 11 Cohort Lands The cohort's own landing at the Group Level 12 Long Obedience Closing the arc; the long road ahead The arc Going Out has four blocks of three weeks each, tracing the Acts 1:8 geography of witness — from the immediate context outward. Body Sent (Weeks 1–3). The cohort returns from the interlude, names the shift from interior formation to outward witness, and each member articulates one specific sentence naming where their witness is being directed this season. Mission Close to Home (Weeks 4–6). The witness in the daily relational world: the data of the weekly Tells, the household, and the vocational context. Mission Far (Weeks 7–9). The broader geography: third places, the cohort's corporate discernment at Week 8, and the sending with hands laid on. Sending & Re formation (Weeks 10–12). What was produced is named honestly — individually, then as a body — and the series closes with a sending into a long obedience the team walks alongside for six to twelve months. On where the body is sent The handbook is explicit: everyone is sent — but not everyone is sent to start a group. When the cohort discerns together at Week 8, the honest landings are several, and held as equal: a specific shared engagement the cohort takes on as a body; differentiated individual callings — a deeper household season, a vocational long obedience, a sustained third place arc, a one to one accompaniment, a contemplative and largely hidden shape, or a calling to gather a new formation group; or a clarifying question the body carries forward for further work. Acts 13 sent two of the five named at Antioch; the other three were doing real work, just not that work in that moment. The team's discipline is to name a quieter sending as honestly — and as honorably — as a louder one. The formation theology behind this — the upper levels of internalization, where the hundredfold becomes fruit that reproduces, and reproduction is discerned rather than assumed — is developed in the IJH Hearing God Paper BFP — Bearing Fruit with Patience. A separate follow on — Inviting Others — equips those whose Going Out Wk 10 calling surfaces in the group starting direction. It is not a fourth series in the arc; it is the equipping that meets a specific calling when the Spirit confirms one. See the Inviting Others handbook. title: Inviting Others Handbook
text: FELLOWSHIP OF THE HEART Inviting Others series Inviting Others Discerning, equipping, and sending leaders to start formation groups in their own rooms COMPANION HANDBOOK Pilot edition — Covenant Christian Academy of Warrenton Based on the Intentional Journey of the Heart (IJH), Volumes 1–6 John G. Tittle • Curriculum draft v1, May 2026 A Letter to the Companion Welcome to Inviting Others. This handbook is for the team carrying the Inviting Others series at Covenant Christian Academy of Warrenton. Most of you have walked Getting Started and Going Deeper with these families. Some of you are coming in fresh because the work has grown and we need elders on the team — elders in the New Testament sense, not the chronological one. The handbook is written for both of you. Inviting Others is not curriculum. It is the recognition of what the Spirit has already been doing across three prior series, and the communal sending of those He has formed and is now calling to start formation groups of their own. Three things you should know before you read further. First: not everyone who finished Going Deeper will be sent in the Going Out. The discernment phase (Wks 1–4) is a real gate. Some participants will be confirmed to lead; some will be confirmed in supporting roles; some will be counseled toward further formation before any sending. All three are honest outcomes, and the team must be willing to name the third option in front of the cohort. Acts 13 only sent two of the five named in the Antioch passage; the other three were doing real work, just not the work of being apostles in that moment. Second: every sent leader is sent under spiritual authority that is not CCA. Each calling confirmed leader has individual spiritual direction with someone outside CCA, and each new group has a “home” — a church or other spiritual hierarchy that recognizes the group, holds it accountable, and provides ongoing pastoral covering. CCA is the soil that grew the leader; CCA is not the institutional parent of the group. Section 3 of this handbook is explicit about why this matters and what it requires. Third: the goal of Inviting Others is to produce Level 2 leaders — not Level 5. The Affective Taxonomy applied to leadership (Section 4) names five levels of Companion development. Level 5 is multi generational, self replicating leadership; it takes years and the support of a leader’s own ongoing formation to reach. Inviting Others aims at Level 2 with the conditions in place for movement toward Level 3 across the leader’s first 6–12 months of leading. We are not graduating Companion mature leaders; we are setting them honestly on a long road and walking with them for the first six months of it. Walk gently. The leaders being sent this Going Out are people the team has known across three series of formation work; they are also people who are about to bear weight they have not borne before. Honor what they have given you across these months by naming honestly what they are and are not ready for. The work itself is the Spirit’s; we are the room He is using to confirm what He has already started. — John Section 1 — The Series at a Glance Title and theme “Inviting Others.” The title is purposefully active. Getting Started was an introduction; Going Deeper went deeper; Going Out is movement — from the room that formed you to the room you are being sent into. The big idea From MSFIG of IJH: “Group Level 5: Former members lead new groups that exhibit the same hearing culture, not by following a manual but by having been formed by it. The Level 5 culture is portable. It replicates itself through the people it has formed.” Inviting Others is the operationalization of this claim. The series equips people who have been formed by Getting Started + Going Deeper + Going Out to start formation groups of their own, in their own rooms, shaped by the Spirit for those specific rooms. text: FELLOWSHIP OF THE HEART Going Out series Week 1 Welcome Back — Returning to the Sent Body The cohort returns. The gap is named. Going Out opens with a different posture. The session’s primary work is honest landing — what the interlude revealed, who returned, who did not, and what posture the cohort carries into a series whose orientation is outward, not inward. WEEK 1 — WELCOME BACK / RETURNING TO THE SENT BODY (90 minutes) Aim. Reopen the cohort after the interlude. Surface what the interlude revealed in each member. Frame Going Out’s posture: Going Out is not a sequel to Going Deeper but a different kind of work — the body sent, oriented outward, with formation now feeding mission rather than the other way around. Re establish container conditions; re engage standing pairs (continuing Going Deeper pairs + new pairs for new continuers if any); set practices for Going Out. Anchor scripture. Acts 1:8 (you shall receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you, and you shall be my witnesses); Hebrews 12:1–2 returning (the joy set before Him; the body running with endurance toward the joy). Connect focus. Sent. The body together discerning what it has been formed for and how the Spirit is leading it outward. Mode. Whole room. No cohort split tonight. The cohort returns as one body — the cohort that walked Going Deeper together is now reassembled to begin Going Out as that same body, even with adjustments. Center. Each member shares briefly the question they carried across the interlude (from H11.3 prompt 4 of Going Deeper) and one sentence about how the interlude landed. Lead Companion frames Going Out’s four block architecture and Going Out’s different posture. Standing pair re engagement / new pair formation. Brief Acts 1 teaching. Between session practice. Daily Rhythm Card practices continue (carried across the interlude). The question carried from H11.3 prompt 4 is brought to the standing pair this week for renewed processing in light of Wk 1’s framing. Each member sits with: ‘Where might I already be sent, that I had not noticed?’ IJH source. Acts 1:1–8 (the architectural anchor); Acts 13:1–3 (the body that worshipped, fasted, and was sent); Vol 2 Exp 9 (Community as Amplifier — community structurally required for full spiritual operation, including for genuine outward witness); Hebrews 12:1–2 returning (‘the joy set before him’ read as missional rather than merely eschatological). WATCH FOR (Week 1 specific risks — read twice) The risks tonight are not primarily clinical. They are pastoral and architectural. The interlude have produced different kinds of landings in different members; tonight’s framing must hold them all without collapsing to the average. The participant who lost momentum across the interlude. The Rhythm Card practices may have lapsed; the question from H11.3 may have faded; the participant may arrive feeling behind. Receive without alarm. Going Out re roots the practices; the question can be re found. Cohort Companion follow up within the week. The participant whose gap surfaced something larger than expected (a vocational rupture, a relational crisis, a health diagnosis). Receive without making it the cohort’s focus tonight. text: FELLOWSHIP OF THE HEART Going Out series Week 2 What It Means to Be Sent Acts 2 and 1 Peter 2 — the empowered body becomes outward witness COMPANION LESSON PLAN Pilot edition — Covenant Christian Academy of Warrenton Based on the Intentional Journey of the Heart (IJH), Volumes 1–6 John G. Tittle • Curriculum draft v1, May 2026 Quick Reference Card Print this page on cardstock. Two copies in the room. Wk 2 teaches the theology and architecture of the sent body, then engages the cohort in its first explicit witness exercise of Going Out. WEEK 2 — WHAT IT MEANS TO BE SENT (90 minutes) Aim. Walk the New Testament architecture of the sent body — Acts 2 (Pentecost; the Spirit empowers the gathered body for outward witness) and 1 Peter 2:9–10 (a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for his own possession). Distinguish witness from evangelism, witness from program, witness from performance. Each member begins to discern: what kind of sent body am I a member of, specifically? Anchor scripture. Acts 2:1–4, 38–41 (Pentecost; the Spirit’s arrival as empowerment for witness); 1 Peter 2:9–10 (the body’s identity as a sent people); Matthew 28:18–20 returning briefly (the great commission read in light of the Acts 2 empowerment, not separate from it). Connect focus. Sent. The architecture of being sent, before the specifics of where each member is sent (which is Wk 3’s work). Mode. Whole room. The teaching block is shared; the witness exercise (Block 5) is shared; closing is shared. Center. Acts 2 + 1 Peter 2 teaching (20 min). Then a witness exercise: each member, around the circle, briefly names one specific person (initials only) to whom they have been a witness across the past week’s practice (the H1.2 outside cohort Tell). What was the Tell; what was true about it; what surfaced. The cohort listens together. Between session practice. Daily noticing question intensifies: ‘Where this week am I already a witness, even unintentionally?’ Continue the weekly Tell outside the cohort. Standing pair check in this week: ‘What is the kind of sent body you sense the Spirit is making YOU specifically? Not where you are sent yet — what kind of witness?’ IJH source. Acts 2 (Pentecost as the body empowerment paradigm); 1 Peter 2:9–10 (the corporate identity of the sent body); proposed Vol 1 Exploration on baptism in the Holy Spirit as empowerment for witness (distinct from regeneration); Vol 2 Exp 9 (Community as Amplifier — the body sent together amplifies witness, just as it amplifies hearing). The vocabulary of ‘witness’ carries baggage in many traditions; the architecture must hold without collapsing into either evangelism as program or witness as performance. Witness collapsed into evangelism as program. Some members may default to a ‘how to share my faith’ frame they learned elsewhere. The architecture is more specific: witness is the body’s outward expression of what the Spirit has formed in it. Programs are tools; witness is identity. Re frame gently when this collapse happens. Witness performed as proof of growth. Some members may report this week’s Tell as evidence of their formation. The architecture is the opposite — the witness IS the formation, lived; not its proof. text: FELLOWSHIP OF THE HEART Going Out series Week 3 Where Am I Being Sent Cohort split discernment — each member articulates a specific sent context using the language of gift, shadow, calling, and witness COMPANION LESSON PLAN Pilot edition — Covenant Christian Academy of Warrenton Based on the Intentional Journey of the Heart (IJH), Volumes 1–6 John G. Tittle • Curriculum draft v1, May 2026 Quick Reference Card Print this page on cardstock. Two copies in the room. Wk 3 closes the body sent block. The cohort splits; each member articulates a specific sent context drawing on Going Deeper’s gift / shadow / calling work and the past two weeks’ witness emergence; the cohort merges to share. WEEK 3 — WHERE AM I BEING SENT (90 minutes) Aim. Each cohort member articulates a specific sent context for Going Out — a particular relational world, vocational context, or service rhythm where the Spirit is calling them to engage as a witness this season. The articulation draws on Going Deeper Wk 9 (gift and shadow), Going Deeper Wk 10 (Acts 13 calling integration where applicable), the Going Deeper H11.3 prompt 4 question, and the past two weeks of outside cohort Tells. The cohort holds the body of named contexts together as the foundation for Wks 4–9’s mission close to home and mission far blocks. Anchor scripture. Acts 13:1–3 (the body discerns and sends); 1 Corinthians 12:4–7 (varieties of gifts, varieties of service, the same Spirit, for the common good); Ephesians 2:10 (we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works which God prepared beforehand). Connect focus. Sent. The discernment of WHERE the witness is being made specific in each member’s life this season. Mode. Cohort split into junior teens / senior teens / parents (45 min each, parallel). The merge for shared circle close (15 min). Standing pairs do their work first within each cohort space. Center. Each member writes ONE sentence naming a specific sent context for Going Out — a place, a rhythm, a relational world. The standing pair walks the sentence with each other (12 min per direction). The cohort circle hears each member’s sentence around the room (15–20 min). Cohort Companion captures contributions on a flip chart for the merge. Between session practice. Daily noticing question shifts: ‘Lord, am I in the place you are sending me, or am I avoiding it?’ Continue the weekly Tell outside the cohort — ideally now from within the named sent context. Standing pair check in this week: ‘What is one specific obstacle the Spirit is showing you in your sent context?’ Wk 4 begins mission close to home. IJH source. Acts 13:1–3 (Antioch sending — the body discerns specific sending); Going Deeper Wk 9 (gift and shadow as the substrate of witness); Going Deeper Wk 10 (Acts 13 calling discernment for one Discerner becomes the architectural template here for everyone). title: Week 5 — The Household Witness
text: FELLOWSHIP OF THE HEART Going Out series Week 5 The Household Witness The costliest close to home context — family of origin and present household witness; standing pairs do harder work COMPANION LESSON PLAN Pilot edition — Covenant Christian Academy of Warrenton Based on the Intentional Journey of the Heart (IJH), Volumes 1–6 John G. Tittle • Curriculum draft v2, May 2026 (household as calling configuration named) Quick Reference Card Print this page on cardstock. Two copies in the room. Wk 5 engages the household domain — typically the costliest close to home witness context. The cohort splits; standing pairs do substantive pair work on the household witness; cohort circles surface patterns; the merge brings the body together briefly. WEEK 5 — THE HOUSEHOLD WITNESS (90 minutes) Aim. Engage the household domain — family of origin and present household — as a specific sent context for each cohort member. Surface what the past week’s household domain Tell revealed; walk the standing pair through the harder material the household surfaces; receive the cohort circle’s honest range; close briefly as a body. Anchor scripture. Deuteronomy 6:4–9 (the Shema — the household formation mechanism); Acts 16:31–34 (the Philippian jailer’s household conversion — the household as a unit of witness and formation); 1 Timothy 5:8 (‘if anyone does not provide for his relatives, and especially for members of his household, he has denied the faith’); 1 Peter 3:1–2 (witness without a word — specifically in marriage, but applicable broadly to long household relationships). Connect focus. Mission close to home, household domain. Where the witness is most exposed because the receivers know the witness’s history. Mode. Cohort split into junior teens / senior teens / parents (60 min each, parallel). The merge for shared circle close (10 min). Center. Brief teaching frame (10 min). title: Home
text: Fellowship of the Heart — CCA Pilot Three series, walked one weekly evening at a time. The pilot edition of Fellowship of the Heart , the operational expression of the Intentional Journey of the Heart (IJH) framework, prepared for the first Covenant Christian Academy of Warrenton cohort beginning Fall 2026. Coming from A Church Prepared for Revival ? That book — A Church Prepared for Revival: A Pilot Proposed — proposes Fellowship of the Heart as the way a church builds its small group leadership before revival arrives: the vessel before the rain. The three series below are the mechanics it points to, and Getting Started is where a leadership circle would begin. The pilot is organized as three sequential series the cohort walks together, with shared participant materials supporting all three: Series Length Focus 1 Getting Started 22 weeks (a club year) The Four Connects — Self, Others, God, Mission 2 Going Deeper 12 weeks Diagnostic, therapeutic, developmental work of IJH Volume 2 3 Going Out 12 weeks The body sent — discerning and equipping leaders for new groups Read the series in order — each builds on what the cohort has already lived. A cohort that completes only Getting Started has done real work; the deeper series are for those the Spirit prepares to keep walking. Shared participant materials The shared section holds the participant facing artifacts used across all three series: Personal Heart Journal — the daily companion for the whole journey Family Conversation Cards — forty cards organized around the Four Connects Rhythm Card — the daily/weekly/monthly practice card Reading List — annotated guide for parents, teens, and the curious What each series contains Every series follows the same shape: A landing page opening the series and laying out the weeks. A Handbook for the Companion team — the long form context, the theology, the protocols. Weekly Companion Lesson Plans — Quick Reference Card, WATCH FOR, Session at a Glance, Pre Work, Materials, Detailed Run Sheet, Block by Block Scripts, Between session practice, and the IJH source pointer for each session. A CHANGELOG tracking what has shifted between versions. The lesson plans are written for the Companion team. They are detailed on purpose. A new Companion preparing for a heavy session should not be guessing at what to do when the room goes quiet, when a teen weeps, when a parent tries to fix what they should be receiving. The page is a floor under your feet, not a script you read from. Cadence and logistics Series length. Getting Started is a twenty two week club year; Going Deeper and Going Out are 12 weeks each. With breaks between series, the full pilot runs across two school years. Session length. On the CCA pilot's clock, standard sessions are 75 minutes (Wednesdays 4:15–5:30 PM; the school day releases the room at 4:00 and the first fifteen minutes are the room build). Week 21's family commissioning extends to 6:15 — flagged in its lesson plan. A body meeting in the evening will find the plans breathe easily back out to ninety minutes. Companion team. A Lead Companion plus a Co Companion team. In Getting Started (the v1.4 family integrated pilot edition), working weeks share opening and teaching whole room, move into FAMILY CLUSTERS — whole families together, parents first on sharing practices — for the experiential center, and merge for closing. Going Deeper and Going Out retain the split and merge structure with age and role circles. Participants. Parent–teen pairs, individuals, and households. See each series landing page for the specific fit of that series. Status Curriculum draft, May 2026. Pilot edition for the first Covenant Christian Academy cycle (Fall 2026 onward). These materials will change as the cohort teaches us where they are right, where they bend, and where they break. Each series has its own CHANGELOG. title: Companions and Coverings
text: FELLOWSHIP OF THE HEART Shared materials — all three series Companions and Coverings What this work is, and is not — who vouches for a Formation Companion Based on the Intentional Journey of the Heart (IJH), Volumes 1–6 John G. Tittle • Pilot edition, July 2026 The question this page answers Sooner or later someone asks the reasonable question: who certifies a Formation Companion? A parent asks it one way — "who trained you?" A school asks it another way — "what's the credential?" A church in another town asks it a third way — "can we borrow one of yours?" The answer is worth saying carefully, because we refuse it on purpose: no one licenses a Formation Companion, and no one ever will from here. There is no registry, no certificate, no title that travels, no fee for standing. This page says what we do instead, and why. What we are Three things, and only three. A published curriculum. The books, the handbooks, the lesson plans, the cards — open to anyone, free to read and free to run. We received this without paying; we hand it on the same way (Matt. 10:8). A formation pattern. Companions are not trained; they are formed — by receiving every practice before leading it, by second runnings in front of the room, by the Labs, by a covering that watches. The pattern is written down so that any local body can run it on its own people. That is not a limitation of the pattern; it is the pattern (2 Tim. 2:2 — entrusted to the faithful, who entrust it again). A steward of the texts. Over time, a small council keeps the written pattern honest — versions, corrections, integrity of the canon. It stewards pages . It will never steward persons . What we are not We are not a licensing body, a credentialing organization, or a certifying institute — not now, and not when the work grows. This is a refusal, not an oversight, and it stands on three legs: Trust that is real lives close to the ground. A credential is a promise made to strangers by an office far away. But formation is witnessed up close or not at all. Any structure distant enough to certify people it cannot see is distant enough to be wrong about them — and too distant to weep with them. Authority in this work stays where the weeping can happen. A certificate bends the formation. The moment a certificate exists, people begin forming toward the certificate — performing for the gatekeeper instead of becoming the person. The desire question, the vital signs, the honest dry season: all of it corrupts when standing depends on displaying it well. Hands are laid on locally in Scripture. Timothy was told not to be hasty in laying on hands (1 Tim. 5:22) — and the hands are always someone's , someone near enough to know the life. The character tests for leaders (1 Tim. 3, Titus 1) are written to be applied by people who can actually observe: household, reputation, years. There is no New Testament office that certifies workers it has never eaten with. The unit of trust is the covering A Formation Companion's standing is exactly this: a named covering, close enough to see their life, says so — and keeps saying so only as long as they can see it. The commissioning at the end of a series (the Week 22 rite, and its like) is that covering's public word about a person they watched form. It is a sending , not a certificate. It means everything inside the household that witnessed it. It claims nothing anywhere else. The same nearness that grants standing can withdraw it. The covering that laid hands on a Companion can take them off — quietly, locally, restoratively where possible. No distant board is needed for this, and none could do it as well. If your body has no Companion Then build your own, from your own people — that is what the written pattern is for . Take your steadiest people; have them receive every practice before they lead one; run the second runnings and the Labs; put them under your own covering; commission them yourselves when your own eyes are satisfied. Pick a card. Read the question aloud. Each person answers, in their own time, in their own way. The card itself does the work — you do not need to add coaching or steer the conversation. title: Interrogating Reality Card
text: FELLOWSHIP OF THE HEART Going Deeper series Interrogating Reality Card Naming what the cohort already knows but has not yet said Based on the Intentional Journey of the Heart (IJH), Volumes 1–6 John G. Tittle • Pilot edition, draft What this is A corporate knot is something a cohort (or a family, or a church) already senses but has — without ever deciding to — agreed not to say aloud: the gap between what we profess and how we treat each other, the fear no one names, the thing everyone is making up stories about. It is the between us cousin of the individual knots the Going Deeper work already addresses one heart at a time. This card is the practice for naming such a thing safely , locating it, and bringing it to the Lord together. It is the reusable, portable form of what Week 8 — the cohort hears itself does live, and it leans on the same I heard discernment discipline the cohort learned in Week 7 — corporate listening prayer . Anchor scripture. "Buy the truth and do not sell it" (Prov 23:23). The body is one with many members, and each sees in part (1 Cor 12:12–27; 1 Cor 13:9–12). "Speaking the truth in love" (Eph 4:15; cf. Matt 18:15). "Be still, and know" (Ps 46:10). Where two or three are gathered, He is in the midst (Matt 18:20); and the others weigh what is heard (1 Cor 14:29). Why the unsaid does not stay gone What a body will not say, it does not stop knowing — it converts into story. An unspoken reality does not dissolve; people fill the silence with assumption and act on the story rather than the truth. Naming it is how the body returns to what is real, so that the Lord can speak into the real thing. The four guards (do not open it without these) 1. The container and the skill are built first. The deep naming is the last move, never the opening one. The cohort earns it across the weeks of reflective listening and the I heard frame. Never cold. 2. Bounded power in the room. People will not name a thing that indicts those with power over them while those people sit there — the silence is the knot, operating. We do not flatten the room; we submit the conversation to the one Head under whom every member sits (1 Cor 12; Eph 1:22–23). Where that submission is not yet real, go to the standing pair 1:1 route below. 3. Voluntary. No one is required to speak or to disclose. 4. A clean close is possible. Work opened and not closed dissipates rather than integrates. Do not open what the gathering has no time or capacity to close. The movements 0. Build the container and the skill — across Going Deeper (reflective listening; the I heard discipline of Wk 7). 1. Ground truths. Each member names what is real for them ; a partner reflects back what they heard before anyone responds. We are assembling the parts, not winning. 2. Name it, and locate its level. Put the knot plainly on the table, then ask whose it is: this cohort? a pair? those who lead? or how this gathering is being led ? Naming the wrong level mis fires the work. 3. Let silence do the heavy lifting. After it is named, do not rush to fill the silence (Ps 46:10). The Companion holds the container open — the same discipline as Wk 7's silent listen. 4. Bring it to the Lord, not just into the room. The gathered cohort brings the named knot before Him (Matt 18:20) and listens for what He is saying about us, weighing what surfaces (1 Cor 14:29; discernment of voices). This is the Wk 8 move: the body hearing about itself. The Spirit, not the technique, does the work. 5. Commitments, accountability, and a clean close. Each names what they will do, with whom, by when; the cohort may hold one another to it (the Tell). Then close the container deliberately — name what was received, honor those who spoke into risk, release. Fallback — when the room cannot hold it. If the naming produces only silence, or power makes candor unsafe, drop to the standing pair 1:1 : ask each member privately "why the silence?" and "what is the real knot here?" , then resurface to the cohort aggregated

title: Keeping the Flame
text: FELLOWSHIP OF THE HEART Shared materials — all three series Keeping the Flame For every Companion, adult or FC1 — how a calling survives its own success Based on the Intentional Journey of the Heart (IJH), Volumes 1–6, and A Church Prepared for Revival John G. Tittle • Pilot edition, July 2026 Why this card exists There is a kind of falling away that never misses a session. The letter to Ephesus describes it exactly: works, toil, patient endurance — all commended — "but I have this against you, that you have abandoned the love you had at first" (Rev. 2:4). A Companion can drift with the room still running beautifully, because leader drift almost always looks like improvement : prep gets faster, sessions get smoother, nothing goes wrong. Polish is what is left when hunger leaves. This is the occupational hazard of handling holy things regularly. Malachi's priests were still offering the sacrifices when they started saying "what a weariness this is" (Mal. 1:13). What was fire the first time becomes procedure by the tenth — not because anyone sinned, but because that is what fire does when nobody tends it. Which is why Scripture's instruction assumes the danger is universal: "fan into flame the gift of God" (2 Tim. 1:6). Flames bank down by default. Rekindling is deliberate. This card is the tending. The Signs Card is for the season when the practices go dry; this card is for the subtler season when the practices go fine — and the wanting quietly retires. The one question, leaders' edition The Signs Card's sorting question works on Companions unchanged: which way does the desire point? A dry season aches toward God — the distance hurts, the wanting is alive. That is the tide, and the Signs Card handles it; dryness is not drift. Satisfaction is different: the role tastes fine without the ache. The sessions satisfy. The competence satisfies. The calling stopped hurting — and you did not notice, because nothing was wrong. The Companion's tells — a self check No one else can run this check on you, and no one should. Once a cycle, alone before God, honestly: I prepare from memory now, and prayer has quietly fallen out of the preparation. Sessions run well — and I have stopped expecting God to actually do anything tonight. I talk about the practices more than I privately do them. When someone in my circle has a breakthrough, what stirs in me is professional satisfaction, not worship. I have not told anything costly, to anyone, in months. I cannot remember the last time I was led — the last time I received a practice as a sheep instead of running it as a shepherd. One of these, in a tired season, is a tired season. Three or more, holding steady while everything runs smoothly — that is the flame banking down. The five defenses 1. Rebuild your own Rhythm Card every cycle — in your own handwriting. The first competency of a Companion is that your own formation is real and ongoing, not technique over an empty interior. So do what the cohort does in Week 15: a fresh card, honest, not idealized — what am I actually practicing now? A leader running last year's rhythm from memory is already coasting. 2. Stay a sheep somewhere. Every shepherd needs a room where they are only a member — a standing cadence, outside every line of consequence, where you tell the costly things. Being under authority is not the same as having such a room; you can be covered and still have nowhere to be honest. If you lead and have no room like this, finding one outranks everything else on this card. Drift is caught in that room months before your cohort could see it — because the first thing satisfaction kills is the leader's own costly telling. 3. Always carry one unmastered assignment. A calling is fed by load, and satisfaction is often just the symptom of insufficient current challenge — you mastered what you were given and nobody handed you the next edge. title: Measurement Covenant
text: FELLOWSHIP OF THE HEART Shared materials — all three series · For the Companion team and church leadership The Measurement Covenant Signed before any survey, journal prompt, observation note, or tracker touches a single heart Adopts the Guardrails of A Church Prepared for Revival for this fellowship's instruments; based on the Intentional Journey of the Heart (IJH), Volumes 4 and 6 John G. Tittle • Pilot edition, July 2026 Why a covenant Unlike every other card in this folder, this one is not for participants. It is for the people who will hold what the participants entrust to us — the surveys, the pulse checks, the observation notes, the trackers named in each series handbook's Assessment Plan. Those instruments are light by design, but they all touch the same material: the condition of a heart that trusted us enough to answer honestly. Knowledge of hearts, in institutional hands, does not stay neutral on its own. It drifts — toward sorting, then managing, then controlling — and the drift happens slowly enough that everyone involved still believes they are shepherding. Written limits are what hold. So before the first instrument is used, the team signs this covenant; and each year, before it is used again, the team re signs it with the ink of a fresh decision. One sentence governs everything below, and it is the test each signer accepts personally: measure nothing you will not weep over. If you can look at what an instrument shows you about the souls in your care and feel nothing — if a hard result reads to you as a data problem rather than a grief — then you are, in that season, a standoff scientist and not a shepherd, and the measures should live in other hands until your heart is back in the room. This is not a slur on scientists; detachment is a virtue in a laboratory. It is a disqualification in a flock. The Lord Himself delivered the most severe diagnostic verdict in the Gospels — and He delivered it weeping (Luke 19:41–44). That is the posture this covenant binds us to: measurement as an act of love, held by people close enough to the faces to cry over them. The commitments The first seven are the Guardrails of A Church Prepared for Revival , adopted whole for this fellowship and restated here in signable form; read that chapter for the full argument under each. The last three are this fellowship's own extensions. 1. Mirrors, not levers. Anything we learn about a heart is held for that person, never over them. It is not market research, a performance dashboard, or raw material for managing anyone. 2. No scores. Nothing about anyone's interior life is ever graded, ranked, or tied to money, position, platform, or standing — because the moment a spiritual measure carries a reward, people will perform it, and the honest will learn to hide. 3. Consent and daylight. No one's heart is discussed, recorded, or reported upward without their knowledge and consent. Anyone may decline any instrument, decline without penalty, and change their mind later. If we want to understand someone, we sit down with them, in the open, and ask. 4. The least powerful test. Any honest reading of our results must include the view from the least powerful seat in the room — and if no one at the table knows how this fellowship looks from that seat, the honest finding is we do not yet know . 5. The bad news test. Anyone — participant, parent, teen, Companion — must be able to say this instrument is hurting someone or this isn't working , about these very tools, and be honored for saying it. We will ask ourselves annually: what happened to the last person who told us something we did not want to hear? 6. Wounds are not weeds. Low warmth on any instrument is never automatically read as low commitment; some numbness is injury, not immaturity. No instrument response ever licenses pressing into a person's pain uninvited. The person sets the pace of their own disclosure, always. 7. The shepherd's scale. Names stop with the person who knows the faces and pray

title: Path Home Card
text: FELLOWSHIP OF THE HEART Shared materials — all three series Path Home Card Confession, lament, return — the written way back, for anyone who has been away Based on the Intentional Journey of the Heart (IJH), Volumes 1–6 John G. Tittle • Pilot edition, July 2026 Why this card exists Every formation journey worth taking has people who fall away from it. Some drift (the Signs Card names that quiet fade). Some burn out. Some blow it — really blow it — and conclude the room they used to sit in would not want them back. And most churches, without ever meaning to, leave the way back unwritten: there are shelves of material for starting the journey and not one page for returning to it. So the returner has to improvise the hardest walk of their life, alone, guessing at the reception. Not here. This card is the written door. If you have been away — a month, a year, a decade; quietly or spectacularly — this is the way back in, and you should know before you take the first step how it ends: it ends with a feast, not a hearing. "But while he was still a long way off, his father saw him and felt compassion, and ran and embraced him and kissed him" (Luke 15:20, ESV). The father runs. That is the reception. Everything below is just the road. Step one — come as you are, and check which voice brought you The way back begins before any words: it begins with turning toward home at all. And at that first turn, learn to tell two voices apart, because both of them will be talking. Conviction is the Spirit's voice, and it draws you toward home: specific about what happened, hopeful about what comes next, and it gets lighter the closer you get. Shame is the other voice, and it drives you away : vague and global ("you're just like this"), hopeless, and it gets louder the closer you get to the people who love you. Scripture puts the difference in one verse: "godly grief produces a repentance that leads to salvation without regret, whereas worldly grief produces death" (2 Cor. 7:10, ESV). Follow the grief that leads somewhere. The voice telling you the door is barred is not the doorkeeper's voice; the doorkeeper left the door unlatched and the light on. Step two — tell it straight, to God and to one person Confession is not groveling; it is telling the truth out loud , and it is the fastest honest step on the road. To God first, in plain words — no polish, no spin: "I said, 'I will confess my transgressions to the LORD,' and you forgave the iniquity of my sin" (Psalm 32:5, ESV). His side of that transaction is already promised: "If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins" (1 John 1:9, ESV). Then to one trusted person — a Companion, a friend from the old cohort, anyone from this fellowship who knows how to hear a soul. One is enough. This is a sovereign share : you choose the person, you choose how much, and nobody in this fellowship will ever require a public confession or hand your story to anyone else. But do not skip the human half. Sin loves the dark, and a secret return has a way of not lasting; the thing said out loud to one kind face loses half its weight on the spot (James 5:16). Step three — grieve what needs grieving Some returns carry real losses — time, trust, a relationship, a season of life that is simply gone. The world says move on; Scripture says something better: lament . God's own songbook devotes a third of its pages to griefs sung out loud in His direction, which settles the question of whether He can bear to hear yours. Borrow the psalmists' words when you have none (Psalm 51 has walked this exact road; so has Psalm 130: "Out of the depths I cry to you, O LORD"). Take the time the grief actually takes. Lament is not the opposite of faith; it is faith, with tears in its voice, refusing to leave the conversation. text: FELLOWSHIP OF THE HEART Getting Started series — The Four Connects Personal Heart Journal A companion for the journey This journal belongs to: \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ Based on the Intentional Journey of the Heart (IJH), Volumes 1–6 John G. Tittle • Pilot edition, May 2026 A Note Before You Begin This journal is a companion for the Fellowship of the Heart Getting Started series — a twenty two week walk across a club year. It is the small, private place where the work each Wednesday continues into your week. Some of what we do in the room only finds its language between sessions — in the quiet of the morning, in the noticing of the day, in a sentence written down at night that surprises you when you read it back. This journal is yours. The team will not collect it. Your cohort will not see it unless you choose. Nothing in it is required. How the journal is set up Each teaching week has its own section, numbered by its place in the year (Weeks 1–11, 13, 15, 21, and 22). Three of them — Weeks 4, 8, and 10 — are second runnings: they continue the same practice as the week before them, with fresh prompts for what a second pass surfaces. The year's other weeks — the re entries (Weeks 12 and 18), the second running blocks (14 and 19), Family Conversation Night (16), the Float (17), and The Long Walk (20) — carry no new pages: keep using the section you are in, and let the daily practices run. Inside a week you will find: An opening page with the week’s scripture and a brief framing for what we are about to practice. A daily practice page with prompts for each day of the week. Free write space for whatever else surfaces. An end of week reflection — which always ends with the same final question: if you were to teach this week’s practice to someone, what would you tell them? Formulating it for another person is how a week’s learning settles into you. It is the same question the evening’s leader answers aloud at every session’s Leader Feedback Round, and at The Long Walk the seniors stop answering it on paper and teach the room. The pages are not assignments. They are scaffolds. If you write a sentence and stop, that is a complete entry. If you fill the margins, that is also a complete entry. The journal scales to what your week actually has time for. Then write what comes — even if it’s nothing. Even ‘nothing came’ is a complete entry. The pattern recognition develops over weeks, not minutes. title: PROAPT Card
text: FELLOWSHIP OF THE HEART Getting Started series — The Four Connects PROAPT Card A hearing practice in scripture — six steps, one passage at a time Based on the Intentional Journey of the Heart (IJH), Volumes 1–6 John G. Tittle • Pilot edition, May 2026 What PROAPT is PROAPT is a hearing practice, not a Bible study technique. The distinction matters. A Bible study asks: what does this passage mean? PROAPT asks: what is the Spirit saying through this passage to me, today, in my specific life? Both are valuable. PROAPT is the second. The operational verse for the practice is Romans 10:17 (ESV) : "So faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of Christ." The chain is Word → Hearing → Faith . PROAPT is the simplest practice that works the chain. One short passage a day is enough to start. The six steps The acronym matters because the order matters. P — Pray Invite the Spirit to speak before reading. You are approaching the Word as someone who expects to hear , not just to extract information. Common error: skipping it. "I'll just dive in." R — Read Read the passage. To receive, not to analyze yet. Let it land first. Common error: going straight to interpretation before the passage has had time to land. O — Observe Observation has two layers, and the order matters. First, the data. Who is there? What is happening? When? Where? These questions are answered straight from the text — no cross references, no background needed; someone with zero scriptural background can answer every one. In John 4, the woman at the well: the interaction is Jesus and a Samaritan woman; the text says it is about noon; they are at a well; the place is Samaria. Then, the interpretation of the data. What do you notice in what you gathered? What stands out, what is strange or unexpected? In John 4: the woman is surprised that Jesus speaks to her. That is an interpretation — the text shows it rather than says it — and it is pivotal, because it opens the dynamics between a Jew and a Samaritan, and between a man and a woman, in that day. Data first, then interpretation. Interpretation built on gathered data is honest observation; interpretation without the data is usually just what you already thought. Common error: skipping the data and importing what you already think the passage means. A — Apply What does this mean for you , today, specifically ? This is where the general word (the logos ) becomes a specific word (the rhema ). Common error: applying the passage to other people. P — Pray again Bring the application back to God. Tell Him what you heard, what you are willing to do, what you are struggling to be willing to do. Common error: skipping it. The obedience channel opens here. T — Tell Share what you heard with someone — a partner, your cohort circle, a spouse, a friend. The speaking solidifies the hearing and creates accountability. Common error: skipping it. The most often omitted step. The Tell is what makes the hearing land in the world rather than evaporate by morning. How to use the card Print this page on cardstock. Tuck it into your Bible or your Personal Heart Journal. One short passage at a time. A paragraph from the gospels, a single Psalm, a half chapter of an epistle. PROAPT works best with bite sized passages where one Spirit given specific can actually land. Daily during weeks 7–15 of Getting Started. The Personal Heart Journal has a daily PROAPT template on the Week 7 and Week 8 pages. Sustain into the rhythm afterward. The Rhythm Card lists PROAPT as part of the daily / weekly hearing practice the cohort sustains after Getting Started ends. When the practice goes flat Most participants experience the practice going flat at some point — a week of going through the steps and nothing landing. When that happens: Don't quit. Flat seasons are part of the rhythm. The faculty of hearing develops across years, not weeks. Change the passage type. If you've been in epistles, move to a gospel or a Psalm. Volume 5 of the IJH project contains a much fuller bibliography for those who want the deeper sources; this list is the on ramp. The books here are organized by Connect, with a small fifth section on integration and rhythm. Each entry has a brief annotation, a tag for who it is for, and a note about when in the journey it is most useful. Not every book is for every reader; pick what fits your season. On reading well Pick one book at a time. Two books in parallel is normal; six books in parallel is a way to read nothing well. Read with a pen. Underline what lands. Write a sentence in the margin when something disagrees with you. Bring what you read to your weekly partner. “Here is a thing I read this week that has stayed with me.” Ten minutes of conversation with one person about a book is worth more than five chapters read alone. Skip what does not land. Return to it in five years. Some books are right for the wrong season; the same book can be exactly right later. If a book unsettles you, that is data. Do not abandon a book just because it is uncomfortable; sometimes the discomfort is the work. But also do not finish a book that is producing harm. title: Rhythm Card
text: FELLOWSHIP OF THE HEART Getting Started series — The Four Connects Daily / Weekly / Monthly Rhythm Card A long term practice for the journey, after Getting Started Based on the Intentional Journey of the Heart (IJH), Volumes 1–6 John G. Tittle • Pilot edition, May 2026 Why a rhythm The Getting Started series taught practices. This card is what the practices become — a durable rhythm of life that holds the four Connects in real time across decades, not weeks. From Vol 2 of IJH: a man who has named his interior, has at least one person who knows his story, has the discipline of hearing scripture as the Spirit speaks, and is walking in what was prepared for him is in a different kind of life than a man who is doing none of these. The difference is not effort; it is rhythm. The man who has the rhythm has it because he set it on purpose and has returned to it many times. The man without it does not have the rhythm because nobody helped him build one. This card is the rhythm. Print it. Stick it on your bathroom mirror or your dashboard or the inside of your journal cover. Customize the specifics. Sustain it across the interlude until Going Deeper begins, and then keep it across the seasons that follow. On returning You will fall away from this rhythm. Most of us do, several times a year, sometimes for weeks at a time. When you fall away, do not start over from the beginning. Just begin again on the next available day. Streaks are not the goal. Returning is the goal. The pattern of returning, over years, is what shapes a life. A man who has returned to the morning question fifty times after fifty falls is in a different relationship with God than a man who never started. Two companions to this page live in the same folder. If the practices have gone dry — you are showing up but the lights are off — read the Signs Card before you read anything into the dryness. And if you have been away a long while and the way back feels barred, the Path Home Card is the door. On scope The rhythm below is the structure. The specifics are yours. A retired grandfather and a high schooler will live this rhythm in different shapes — different times of day, different durations, different weekly partners, different monthly clearings. The structure is universal; the specifics are particular. If a piece of the rhythm does not fit your season — you have a newborn and the morning question is competing with infant feedings, you are in finals and the monthly clearing time is impossible — do not abandon the whole rhythm. Keep what is doable; return to the rest when the season changes. Daily Five to fifteen minutes a day. Two practices that take five minutes each. One optional practice that takes ten to fifteen minutes. The morning question (5 min) Practice Before you check your phone, sit somewhere quiet for five minutes with this question: “Father, what are you up to today — and what do you want me to notice?” Wait sixty seconds. Then write what comes — even if it’s nothing. Even ‘nothing came’ is a complete entry. The pattern recognition develops over weeks, not minutes. Why the morning Because the day has not yet shaped you. Because your phone has not yet shaped you. Because you are at your most receptive in the first ten minutes after waking, and the question gets to occupy the most impressionable real estate of your day. If your morning is genuinely impossible — small children, early commute, night shift schedule — pick another moment that has the same quality. The first quiet ten minutes after the rush has settled. The walk into the office. The first cup of coffee at the desk. Not the literal morning, but the first available pre formed quiet of the day. Common variations Two minute version, when five is impossible. The question, sixty seconds of waiting, one written sentence. That is enough to keep the practice alive. title: Signs Card
text: FELLOWSHIP OF THE HEART Shared materials — all three series Signs Card When the practices go dry — four kinds of dry, and how to tell them apart Based on the Intentional Journey of the Heart (IJH), Volumes 1–6, and A Church Prepared for Revival, Movement III John G. Tittle • Pilot edition, July 2026 Why this card exists Sooner or later, everyone who works the Rhythm Card hits a season where the practices go gray. Prayer feels like talking to the ceiling. Scripture reads like cardboard. The garden is just a chair. When that season comes, the most dangerous thing in the room is not the dryness. It is the wrong diagnosis — the voice (sometimes another person's, usually your own) that says dryness means failure, or fake faith, or a God who looked at you and left. Whole journeys have ended over a misread dry season. This card exists so that never happens to anyone in this fellowship. Dryness is usually the tide, and only sometimes the thorn. The tide goes out and comes back; that is how seas work, and how souls work. This card is for telling the tide from the things that are not the tide. The one question that sorts everything Which way does the desire point? Not how do you feel — feelings are exactly what have gone quiet. The question is underneath the feelings: when you are honest, do you still want God — do you miss Him, does the distance ache — or has the wanting itself faded and the world tastes fine without Him? That single question separates four different kinds of dry, and they need different responses. Two of them even command opposite motions, which is why this card must be learned before the dry season and not improvised inside it. The four kinds of dry 1. Neglect 2. Worn out 3. The enemy's dry wind 4. God's own stripping Desire for God Faded; the distance doesn't ache Buried under duty; you want escape, not God Under assault; you feel accused and pressured Intact and starving — the ache is the sign Rest of life The world still tastes fine Restless churn; "anywhere but here" Urgency, fear, secrecy The world has gone gray too; nothing else satisfies either The practices Quietly lapsed, and you don't grieve them Frantic or duty driven, joyless You're tempted to quit and undo good decisions You keep showing up, and it feels like nothing The tell No ache at all The "I'd be better off elsewhere" whisper A voice counseling change: quit, undo, leave Painful worry about failing God — lukewarm hearts never worry about that First step Wake and turn; rebuild the rhythm (James 4:8) Rest; lighter yoke; stay put; smaller faithful steps (Matt. 11:28–30) Resist : change nothing, pray a little more, tell someone (1 Pet. 5:8–9) Receive : wait, stay faithful, stay accompanied (Job 23:10) Notice cases 3 and 4: one says fight , the other says yield . Getting them backwards — fighting God's stripping, or yielding to the enemy's wind — is the costliest mistake in the dry country. When you cannot tell which one you are in, do not decide alone. That is what Companions are for. The rules of the card 1. This card is for your own heart, and for one trusted person to help you read it. It is never a tool for diagnosing somebody else's soul at a distance. Nobody gets filed under a column. 2. In every case, tell someone. Darkness spoken aloud loses half its weight. Dryness that stays hidden is the kind the research says goes bad; dryness that is spoken, met without a verdict, and companioned is the kind that becomes root system. 3. Make no big decisions in the dark. No quitting, no leaving, no undoing of things decided in the light — until the light returns. 4. Know when to call the doctor. If the gray has swallowed everything — sleep, appetite, humor, compassion — or there is self loathing or any talk of self harm, that is a treatable illness, not a spiritual verdict. title: Three Vital Signs
text: FELLOWSHIP OF THE HEART Shared materials — all three series The Three Vital Signs The Companion team's weekly lens — three readings, taken in ordinary time, that tell you how a body is actually doing Based on the Intentional Journey of the Heart (IJH), Volumes 1–6, and A Church Prepared for Revival John G. Tittle • Pilot edition, July 2026 Why this card exists A fellowship can drown in measurement. The assessment plan behind this pilot has surveys, journals, observation notes, and a research framework several volumes deep — and a Companion in an ordinary Wednesday session needs almost none of it. A doctor takes four vital signs at every visit and orders the deeper tests only when one of them is off. This card is the Companion's version: three signs, watchable in an ordinary session, with no form in anyone's hand. Everything else in the assessment plan is the deeper workup — used rarely, gently, and only when a vital sign says to look closer. The three signs are not three separate things. Underneath them is one thing: confidence in God in the middle of suffering, noise, and even disaster. Hope that is anchored in Him, not in outcomes — the "but if not" of the three men at the furnace (Dan. 3:17–18), who knew God was able to deliver them and had already decided how they would stand if He didn't. That kind of hope cannot be read on a survey taken on a calm night, because it only shows itself under load. So the signs are read where load actually arrives: in ordinary weeks, with their ordinary interruptions, emergencies, and griefs. Sign 1 — Costly Telling What it is. Someone tells the group what God said and what they did about it — or tells something true that costs them to say. Why it reads so much at once. Telling is obedience made visible — it is the sixth step of PROAPT for a reason. And telling is also the room's safety gauge, because it is the first thing to stop when a room stops being safe. People fall silent long before they walk away. One sign, two readings: is God being heard and obeyed here, and is it safe to say so? What to watch. Does telling happen at all? Does it ever cost anything, or is it all polished? Does it come from more than the same three people? And watch what the room does with a costly tell — receiving it well is the sign at full strength; rushing to fix it is the sign starting to fail. The counterfeit. Performed testimony — frequent, fluent, and free. Count the cost, not the occurrences. Sign 2 — Response to Load What it is. What a person, or the room, does when load arrives — an interruption, an emergency, hard news, real suffering. What to watch. The first ten seconds after a disruption. Does the room absorb it or panic? Do people move toward the trouble or look to the leader to handle it? When you ask someone why — and then ask why again — does the answer deepen, or does it scatter? A settled second answer is experience speaking; a scattered one is a script running out. Tears are not a bad reading. A room that grieves openly and hopes anyway is the sign at its strongest, not its weakest — "sorrowful, yet always rejoicing" (2 Cor. 6:10). What reads low is not grief but despair — and not fear felt, but fear handed around as the verdict. The counterfeit. Presumption — calm that rests on a guaranteed outcome rather than on God. The gentle test, where expectancy runs high: "and what if it doesn't turn out?" Anchored hope has already been to that question. Presumption hasn't, and it shows. Sign 3 — The Sought Stray What it is. When someone goes quiet or goes missing — how long before anyone notices, and who goes after them. Why it earns its place. Jesus made love between members the one sign He said outsiders could read (John 13:35), and the stray no one sought is the first symptom on Scripture's own list of a failing flock (Ezek. 34:4). title: Watching Trust Grow
text: FELLOWSHIP OF THE HEART Shared materials — all three series Watching Trust Grow The Companion's field guide to a room's deepening trust — three ages, six markers, two warnings. You don't need the research; you need to recognize it when you hear it. Based on the Intentional Journey of the Heart (IJH) and the group trust research literature John G. Tittle • Pilot edition, August 2026 Why this card exists Trust is what the Three Vital Signs run on. Costly telling, load borne toward God, strays sought without prompting — those are what trust does when God is in the room. The signs card watches the fruit; this card teaches a Companion to see the trellis. Most Companions have never read the trust research, and none of them need to. What a Companion needs is to recognize trust's ages when they hear them — at a pickup, in a cluster, in the sentence a parent uses to describe the group to a neighbor — because a room announces where it is in its ordinary talk long before any instrument could tell you. Half a century of research compresses to one claim worth carrying: trust grows in stages, each the foundation for the next, and the stage a room's trust has reached is the truest reading of how deeply its life together has gone inward. (For the curious, the bones: the three stages are Lewicki and Bunker's trust development model; several of the watchable markers come from Edmondson's psychological safety research; the deepening disclosure gradient is Altman and Taylor's; the findings about conflict are Wheelan's and Peck's group development work; and a meta analysis of 112 studies places a team's internal trust among the most consequential facts about it. None of that vocabulary ever enters the room.) The three ages of a room's trust One thing, three ages — like the signs' first, growing, and full forms. Every room passes through all three, and no age is a failure; a young room in its young age is a healthy room. HELD — the container holds them What it is. People are honest and kind because the structure holds them there: the covenant, the protocols, the Companion's presence. The room trusts the rules more than it trusts each other yet. Every September room is HELD. What it sounds like. Eyes go to the leader before anyone answers. "Are we allowed to…?" Sharing stays at prayer request distance. Politeness everywhere, disagreement nowhere. When the leader steps out, the room quietly waits. What to do. Keep the container faithful, because trust's first age is built entirely on kept promises: start on time, keep every confidence, let no honest word ever be punished. The container is the scaffolding trust climbs. KNOWN — they know each other now What it is. Enough true exchanges have landed that people can anticipate one another; predictability has become affection's first draft. What it sounds like. Names used across family lines. Gentle teasing that lands soft — "you always say that." Someone quotes what another person shared three weeks ago. Pickup conversations run long between families who arrived as strangers. Predictions about each other — "Maria's going to love this one." A teen asks another family's parent a real question. What to do. Feed it occasions — the clusters, the pairs, the Week 16 table. And start watching for the first disagreement; its arrival is usually good news (see the warnings). OWNED — each other's people What it is. The group's way of being together has been taken inside; members carry the room's values as their own. This is internalization visible at group scale — the room no longer needs holding, because its people have taken the holding into themselves. What it sounds like. "These are my people." "We" quietly replacing "this group." Someone defends an absent member. The room corrects itself without the leader — "hey, let her finish." A teen texts another family's parent when something breaks. text: FELLOWSHIP OF THE HEART Shared materials — team facing The Weekly Run Card Who holds what, next Wednesday — filled in on the Thursday Call, read back aloud, sent to the team before anyone hangs up John G. Tittle • Pilot edition, August 2026 What this card is The team's whole weekly rhythm is one forty five minute call shortly after each Wednesday session — look back, look at the flock, look ahead (Getting Started Handbook, Section 3). This card is the look ahead's product: one page, the same grid every week, that says exactly who holds what at the next session. It is filled in live on the call, the Lead Companion reads it back aloud at the close — every person hears their own name and their own line — and the scribe sends it to the whole team before the call ends. The role names never change; the specifics do. That is what makes the card thirty seconds to fill and impossible to misread. The two rules 1. One name per line. A role with two names has zero owners. If a job genuinely needs two people, split it into two lines. 2. The "this week specifically" column is the card. Not the role name — the specifics. "Cluster Companion" tells Mike nothing; "the and families, and watch the teen who went quiet last week" tells him everything. The Lead Companion's read back at the close of the call is what turns this page from a plan into an agreement. The card does not replace the plan — it distills the plan into names. Heavy weeks — the storytelling weeks' Section 6 re reads, the Week 19 Dry Season teaching to the Companions in Formation, the Week 21 commissioning logistics — get a separate working session scheduled on the card , not a longer call. The Lord bless the team that plans on Thursday what it prays on Wednesday.

title: Start here
text: Start here — for the curious You are at the front door of Fellowship of the Heart . This page is the short answer to: what is this, and how is walking it supposed to bring a person closer to God? What this is Fellowship of the Heart (FotH) is what it looks like when a real cohort walks the work of the Intentional Journey of the Heart together. Three sequential series, across about a year of Wednesday evenings: Getting Started — a twenty two week club year introducing the four Connects: Self → Others → God → Mission, with the Companion in Formation track (senior teens learning to lead) built into the map. Going Deeper — twelve weeks of the harder interior work, and learning to hear God as a body. Going Out — twelve weeks of the body sent: into household, vocational, third place contexts, and sometimes into starting new formation groups. Plus the shared participant materials — the Personal Heart Journal, the Family Conversation Cards, the Rhythm Card, the Reading List — that walk alongside all three series. The Intentional Journey of the Heart (IJH) sits behind FotH. IJH is the six volume record of how God's love actually works in a human heart — the operative laws, the diagnostics for where you are, the practices that move you forward. FotH is what those volumes look like when a cohort actually walks them. IJH is the what and the why ; FotH is the how and the with whom . The six volumes: Volume 1: Laws of the Spirit — the 46 Foundational Laws (38 of wide consent — cause and effect relationships affirmed across mainstream Christian tradition — plus eight newer ones still being tested), and eight personal Explorations of less mapped territory. The structural and operational laws underneath the spiritual life. Volume 2: Knowing to Doing — the diagnostic, therapeutic, and developmental work — the Heart Soil, the Emotional Knots, the Container, the Tool Map, PROAPT, the Four Connects, the Training Plan. FotH is the cohort walked operational form of Vol 2 most directly. Volume 3: Spiritual Dynamics — the most speculative of the volumes; attempts to translate Vol 1's structural laws into more formal mathematical and dynamical language. Skippable on a first pass unless you enjoy that frame. Volume 4: Testing Framework — how to test all of this in real life, at individual, small group, and larger study scales. Volume 5: References — annotated bibliography, the Periodic Table of Spiritual Laws (the catalog organizer), the Formation Documents (the academic register companion papers — including MSFIG and the four part Hearing God Papers , which measure spiritual maturity in hearing God, prescribe its cultivation, and form the heart through the lower and upper levels of internalization), and the operational tool protocols Companions deploy in sessions. Volume 6: Governance — the framework under which the work is stewarded, extended, and corrected by others beyond the original author. The institutional layer that helps the work outlast its author. Every claim in IJH carries one of three confidence tiers, named explicitly so you can read with the right posture: Clearly Taught — multi author, multi Testament scriptural support; broadly accepted across mainstream Christian traditions. High confidence claims you can operate in. Reasonably Inferred — derivable from scripture by sound reasoning and consistent with experience, but not stated explicitly or widely enough to clear the top tier. Held loosely; needs community testing. Speculative — interesting enough to pursue, not yet solid enough to build on. The IJH site is at jgtittle ministries.github.io/Intentional Journey of the Heart; the Read Me First is the substantive front door. How walking this brings you closer to God The work rests on a claim about how formation actually happens. Most people experience their interior life as noise — feelings, impulses, half formed prayers, things that should be there but aren't. The first thing the journey does is give you words for what is already in you
